claims.text: The starting alloy has a nominally disordered but unoptimized atomic distribution and crystal structure.
Formation of a homogeneous bcc solid solution governs the emergence of superconductivity in the selected alloy.
A homogeneous atomic distribution maximizes configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a simple bcc phase.
Homogeneity combined with local chemical disorder produces locally softened phonon modes.
Local phonon softening enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Superconductivity emerges when electron–phonon coupling exceeds a critical threshold and permits Cooper pairing.
The resulting superconducting state is type II.
Annealing will make the constituent-element distribution more uniform and stabilize the bcc structure.
Moderate hydrostatic pressure will compress the lattice and tune its lattice dynamics.
A superconducting transition is expected in the approximately 2–10 K regime.
Pressure testing up to several tens of GPa is applicable to the proposed low-temperature study.
Electron–phonon coupling is sensitive to local lattice distortions in the stated temperature and pressure regime.
Zero electrical resistance together with a diamagnetic response identifies the superconducting transition.
The treated alloy will have a higher critical temperature and a more robust superconducting state than the untreated alloy.
The critical temperature will correlate with atomic homogeneity and lattice softening.
Less optimal atomic distribution and localized lattice strain in the untreated alloy may suppress or eliminate superconductivity.
The proposed mechanism is limited to simple-structure high-entropy alloys in which chemical disorder strongly affects lattice vibrations and electron–phonon interactions.
Secondary phases, significant segregation, or compositions far from an optimal electron–phonon coupling regime can prevent the hypothesis from applying.
